title: Only Twos, Threes and Fives
statement:
You get an integer n. Return true if n is a positive number whose prime factors are only 2, 3 and 5. Any of the three may appear any number of times, or not at all.

1 has no prime factors at all, so it counts. Zero and negative numbers never count.

examples.why: 60 = 2 · 2 · 3 · 5. Nothing else is left after dividing those out.
42 = 2 · 3 · 7. The 7 is a prime outside the allowed three.
Zero is not positive. A loop that keeps dividing 0 by 2 would never stop, so it has to be rejected first.

hints: If n has only those prime factors, what is left after you remove every 2, every 3 and every 5?
Keep dividing n by 2 while it divides evenly, then by 3, then by 5. The number only qualifies if exactly 1 remains.
Handle n ≤ 0 before the loops: 0 divides by 2 forever and negatives are never allowed.

explain.intuition:
Every positive integer splits into primes in exactly one way. If that split uses only 2, 3 and 5, then dividing out all the 2s, all the 3s and all the 5s leaves nothing but 1. If any other prime is in there, it survives the divisions and the leftover is bigger than 1.

So you do not need to find the other primes. You only strip away the allowed ones and look at what remains.
steps: For each of 2, 3 and 5: while n is divisible by it, divide n by it.
pitfalls: Skipping the n ≤ 0 check. With 0 the division loop never ends.
Returning false for 1. It has no prime factors, so none of them are forbidden.
Checking only that n is divisible by 2, 3 or 5. 14 is divisible by 2 but still has a 7.

solutions.title: Trial division up to the square root
solutions.idea: Find every prime factor by plain trial division and reject the number as soon as one of them is bigger than 5.

solutions.title: Strip the allowed primes
solutions.idea: Divide out every 2, 3 and 5. Only 1 may remain.

followups: Return the k-th positive number that has only these factors. Why does a min-heap or three pointers beat testing every integer?
